4.3

Vertex Form of a Quadratic Function

Facilitation Notes

In this activity, vertex form of a quadratic function is defined. Students analyze
possible equations for parabolas described by a given orientation and the
vertex. Students use technology to graph quadratic functions.
From the graph, they can identify the location of the vertex, identify the
zeros, and rewrite the function in both vertex and factored forms. In the
last activity, several quadratic functions are given, and students use these
equations to state key characteristics.

Have a student read the first paragraph and complete Questions 1
through 3 as a class.
NOTE
Most resources use (h, k) to represent the vertex of a parabola. The theory
is that a, b, c, and d are used for transformations; e is a value used in higher
math classes; f and g are commonly used to denote functions; and i and j are
used for imaginary units. This left the variables h and k available to use for the
coordinates of the vertex.

and Factored Forms

Facilitation Notes
In this activity, a Worked Example shows how to write equations for
quadratic functions in vertex form using the coordinates of the vertex and
another point on the graph. Students write a quadratic equation in factored
form using the zeros and another point on the graph. Students analyze two
methods for writing the same equation using the graph of the function and
use technology to show the equations are the same. They practice writing
equations in vertex form and factored form using different given information.

Question aloud.
Discuss the Worked Example and complete Question 1 as a class.

Summary

A function written in equivalent forms can reveal different characteristics
of the function it defines. You can write a quadratic function in vertex form
when you know the coordinates of the vertex and another point on the
graph. You can write a quadratic function in factored form when you know
the zeros and another point on the graph.

LESSON OVERVIEW

Scissors

Students begin the lesson with an open-ended sort of twelve
mathematical expressions prior to being given the formal definitions
regarding polynomials. The terms polynomial, monomial, binomial,
trinomial, and degree of a polynomial are defined. The graphs of two
functions in context provide meaning to subtraction of functions
and introduce the concept of performing addition and subtraction
of polynomial functions. Students add and subtract functions
both graphically and algebraically within a context. They analyze
polynomial expressions that have been rewritten incorrectly and write
them correctly.
